opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few things going on. The most basic one is that a lot of the properties we actually care about in these models only show up once you have enough compute, enough data, and enough parameters for the model to start using its structure in interesting ways. At small scale everything looks kind of similar. You train a little transformer, you train some alternative, and the loss curves sit roughly on top of each other, or the new thing looks a bit worse. So the natural conclusion is "this doesn't help." But you're measuring in a regime where the model hasn't had the capacity or the training signal to do the thing the architecture was designed to enable.

The second thing is that the transformer has had an enormous amount of co-optimization around it. The hyperparameters, the initialization schemes, the optimizers, the learning rate schedules, the data pipelines, the kernels, the hardware itself, all of that has been tuned for years around one architecture. When you drop in something new and run it with a recipe that was effectively designed for something else, it will underperform almost by default. At small scale you usually don't have the budget to do the same level of tuning for the new idea, so you compare a heavily polished baseline against an unpolished challenger and call it a fair fight.

Third, scaling behavior is really what matters, and you can't read the slope of a curve from one point. Something might be slightly worse at small scale but scale better, with a better exponent or a better constant that only becomes visible after a couple orders of magnitude. Or it might be the opposite: an idea that looks great small and then washes out because it was compensating for something larger models learn anyway. Either way, small experiments are a noisy and sometimes misleading proxy.

And then there's the capability side, beyond loss. Things like reasoning over long horizons, using memory well, or doing reinforcement learning on top of a pretrained model are emergent-ish behaviors. If your architecture is supposed to help with something like long-context reasoning, a small model that can't reason at all won't show you the benefit. You need a model that is already good enough for the advantage to have somewhere to show up.

So I'd say small-scale testing is great for filtering out ideas that are clearly broken, but it's a pretty weak tool for finding the ideas that are going to matter most. That's a big part of why architecture research is hard. The really interesting bets are expensive to evaluate properly, and the field tends to converge on whatever has already been validated at scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, and I think it's one of the more underappreciated problems in the field. The short version is that small-scale experiments measure how fast an architecture learns, not how much it can eventually learn, and those two things are not the same.

When you're at small compute, you're basically in a regime where the model is starving for signal. So anything that gives it a strong inductive bias, anything that bakes in structure about the problem, looks great. It converges faster, the loss curve looks better, you write the paper. But that same structure that helps you at small scale is often the thing that constrains you later. At large scale the model has enough data and enough capacity that it would rather figure out the structure itself, and your clever prior just becomes a ceiling.

Transformers are the classic example. At small scale, LSTMs and convnets were often competitive or better. The transformer didn't look magical when you trained it for a few hours on one GPU. What made it win was that it kept getting better when you threw more at it, and the alternatives flattened out. If you'd been making decisions purely from small compute experiments in 2017, you might have discarded it.

The other thing is that a lot of the behaviors we actually care about are emergent. In-context learning, multi-step reasoning, these things show up at a certain scale and essentially don't exist below it. So if your architecture is specifically good at supporting those behaviors, a small experiment literally cannot see the advantage, because the behavior isn't there yet in any architecture.

And then there's the mundane stuff, which honestly matters a lot. Hyperparameters don't transfer. Learning rate, initialization, the right batch size, all of that changes with scale, and a new architecture usually hasn't had the thousands of hours of tuning that the incumbent has. So you're comparing a well-tuned baseline against something that's badly tuned, and you conclude the new thing doesn't work.

The way I think about handling it is you have to look at scaling trends rather than point estimates. Train a ladder of sizes, even if the biggest one is still small by frontier standards, and look at the slope. Is this thing getting better faster than the baseline as you go up, or is the gap shrinking? That's a much more informative signal than "which one won at ten million parameters." It's more expensive and it's less satisfying, because you often end up saying "we don't know yet," but I think that's the honest answer a lot of the time.

astra-6.text:
Because what you really care about is how an architecture behaves at the scale where you’re going to use it. And a small experiment gives you only one point on that curve. One architecture might learn faster initially, but another might keep improving for longer and eventually overtake it as you add compute and data.

There’s also a tuning problem. Your baseline usually has a lot of engineering behind it—the learning rates, initialization, all those choices. A new architecture might need different choices, so a small test can end up measuring how well you understand how to train it, rather than its ultimate potential.

Small experiments are still useful. But I’d want to see how the gap changes across several scales, rather than reject an idea because it loses at the smallest one.

sol-6.1.text:
Because an architecture that looks worse at a small scale might actually scale better. When you run a small experiment, you’re measuring performance at one particular compute budget. You’re not necessarily learning what happens when you increase that budget by a hundred or a thousand times.

And there’s another complication: we’ve spent a lot of effort tuning the architectures we already use. A new idea might need different hyperparameters or a different training setup. So if you test it using the recipe that works best for the incumbent, you can reject it too early.

Small experiments are useful. But you want to look at the trajectory across scales, rather than assume that whoever wins the smallest experiment will also win the largest one.
